excerpt: "Survival, in those days, was less a matter of courage than of blind luck." Unaware the island had fallen, Yoshio Ideguchi spent months in the dense jungles of Saipan waiting for a war that had already passed him by. Read the personal story of a World War II holdout who turned a site of tragedy into a lifetime of peaceful return.
author: Lexi Zotomayor

bodyText:
Months after Captain Oba Sakae finally descended the mountain to yield his sword, another ghost remained in the shadows of Saipan. I was eighteen when I first set foot on that island, young enough that the fog of war had not yet settled into my bones, though it soon would.

We had sailed out from Yokosuka in early 1944, a bellyful of boys staring out at an endless, dark Pacific. None of us knew where the ship was taking us, only that American submarines were waiting somewhere beneath the swell, silent and patient. When we arrived, the air was thick with heat and the quiet desperation of a military trying to fortify a paradise.

Then came the fire. The American invasion did not feel like a battle so much as a collapse of the sky. Their bombs fell without pause, their guns roared from the tide, and everything we had built was turned to splinters and dust. How I made it back through that initial storm without a scratch is a detail time has mercifully smudged away. Survival, in those days, was less a matter of courage than of blind luck.

For months, the jungle became my entire world. It was a dark, tangled green where time stopped moving. I lived on what the damp earth offered, mostly snails gathered from the underbrush, keeping my breath quiet while the island moved on around me. When the call to surrender finally drifted into the canopy, the words sounded strange, almost foreign to ears accustomed only to the wind and the birds. It was not until a familiar voice—a native speaker pleading with us to step into the light—reached into the thicket that I understood the war was truly over.

I have gone back to Saipan more than thirty times since. The island that once tried to swallow me whole has become a place of quiet reconciliation. On a summer afternoon in 2014, sitting among the elders at the Manamko’ Center, we played music together—their songs, my songs, standard tunes that needed no translation. The jungle has long since reclaimed the bomb craters, and where there was once only relentless noise, there is now just the simple, sweet harmony of people who survived.
title: The Story of Yoshio Ideguchi
